metadata.title: The Measurement of Socio-economic Status in PISA (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This working paper focuses on the measurement quality, scaling, and comparability of socio-economic status indicators (ESCS) in PISA rather than fitting an ML prediction model on a student-level analytic dataset. As such, the paper does not provide enough methodological detail in the excerpt to determine whether complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights and replicate weights) were applied in any specific empirical analyses. For PISA micro-data analyses, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights supplied with the dataset to account for the stratified, clustered design and to obtain correct standard errors. If the paper’s analyses are based on instrument development, field-trial experiments, or scaling validity checks, weighting may be handled within the PISA scaling procedures rather than explicitly reported at the analysis stage.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines how socio-economic status is measured in PISA, focusing on the index of economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and its components. It reviews changes introduced over time in questionnaires (parental education, occupation, household possessions), scaling procedures, and field-trial experiments in 2021 that used alternative question formats. The paper also analyzes trends in ESCS components from 2015 to 2022 to assess whether observed changes reflect real shifts or measurement artifacts. Finally, it evaluates validity, reliability, and comparability of ESCS component measures, including differences between self- vs proxy reports, post-coded vs pre-coded occupation formats, and parent vs student reporting of household possessions. The excerpt does not provide student-level ML model performance metrics or explicit PV/missing-data handling, indicating the work is primarily measurement-focused rather than predictive modeling.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The provided excerpt is a high-level description of a measurement-focused working paper and does not include the empirical modeling details needed to extract an ML pipeline, target variables, performance metrics, or student-level sample sizes. Consequently, fields such as total_students, country-level Ns, and PV/missing-data handling cannot be populated from the excerpt without risking fabrication. The paper’s structure (instrument changes, scaling procedures, field-trial experiments, and validity/comparability checks) supports an exploratory research design centered on measurement quality rather than predictive inference.
